title.en: KV Cache: Why LLMs Don't Recompute Everything Every Token

description.en: Generating text one token at a time sounds like it should recompute everything from scratch, every step. It doesn't — the KV cache is why. See exactly how much redundant work caching removes.

story_variants.en:
## The Waste Nobody Notices

"An LLM generates one token, then another, then another," Vaathiyaar says. "Naively, that means: to generate token 5, re-read tokens 1 through 4 and recompute their **key** and **value** projections from scratch. Then for token 6, redo tokens 1 through 5. Every. Single. Step."

### The Fix: Compute Once, Reuse Forever

A token's key (K) and value (V) projections never change once computed — they don't depend on what comes *after* the token, only on the token itself and everything before it. So instead of recomputing them, a **KV cache** stores each token's K/V the first time it's projected, and every later generation step just reuses that stored result and computes K/V for the *one new token*.

```
without cache: step 1 does 1 projection, step 2 redoes 2, step 3 redoes 3, ...
               total for 5 tokens = 1+2+3+4+5 = 15

with cache:    step 1 does 1 (new), step 2 does 1 (new), step 3 does 1 (new), ...
               total for 5 tokens = 5
```

That gap between 15 and 5 only grows as the conversation gets longer — without a cache, total work scales roughly with the *square* of sequence length; with a cache, it scales linearly. This is the single biggest reason a 2026 chat model can hold a 32K-token conversation and still respond in under a second per token.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** if it was computed before and can't change, cache it. The KV cache is that principle applied to the single most expensive repeated step in autoregressive generation.

Today you implement both counts yourself and measure the savings directly.

uth_example:
prompt = ["The", "cat", "sat", "on", "the", "mat"]

naive_work, cached_work, cache = [], [], []
for step in range(1, len(prompt) + 1):
    naive_work.append(step)                 # re-project every earlier token
    cache.append(f"KV({prompt[step - 1]})")  # project only the new one, keep it
    cached_work.append(1)

naive_total, cached_total = sum(naive_work), sum(cached_work)
saved = round((1 - cached_total / naive_total) * 100, 1)
print("cache:", cache)
print(f"projections: naive {naive_total}, cached {cached_total} -> {saved}% saved")

under_the_hood.summary: Without a cache, generating token t recomputes key and value projections for all t tokens; with a KV cache each token's K and V are projected once and stored, so projection work drops from 1 + 2 + ... + n to n.

steps.title: What a projection is
steps.body: For every token, every layer computes k = x W_k and v = x W_v. These depend only on that token and earlier ones (because of the causal mask), so they never change when later tokens arrive.

steps.title: Count the work without a cache
steps.body: Step 1 projects 1 token, step 2 projects 2, and step n projects n. Generating 5 tokens costs 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15 projections; in general n(n + 1)/2, which grows quadratically.

steps.title: Count the work with a cache
steps.body: Each step projects only the new token and appends its k and v to the cache: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5 projections. For 1,000 tokens that is 1,000 instead of 500,500.

steps.title: Attention still reads everything
steps.body: The new token's query must still be compared with all cached keys, so attention work per step still grows with length. The cache removes the repeated projections and the repeated full forward passes, not the attention lookup itself.

steps.title: The trade
steps.body: Compute saved is paid for in memory: the cache must hold K and V for every past token in every layer. That is why serving systems care so much about cache size.

memory grows with length

under_the_hood.takeaway: Caching works because past keys and values are immutable under the causal mask. Computing each once turns quadratic waste into linear work, at the cost of memory.
